findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State on the FORWARD resize path (not only rollback) that the instance_type change stops/starts the production host, name the expected downtime window, and require the same Gerrit /config/server/version, review-bot /review/health, and MCP /mcp/ health recovery checks before declaring the resize successful.
evidence: Forward frame: 'update aws_instance.gerrit (replace=[]) -- instance type changes from t4g.large to approved r7g.large' and 'the intended mutable field is instance_type only' -- no stop/start or health gate stated for the forward apply.

Rollback path DOES state it: 'allow the required stop/start, then require Gerrit /config/server/version, review-bot /review/health, and MCP /mcp/ response to recover' -- proving a stop/start is known to be required but only documented on rollback.
main.tf:105 warns aws_instance.gerrit 'is the production Gerrit host' and must never force-replace; an instance_type change stops/starts it, causing real downtime.
findings.finding: The forward resize apply requires AWS to stop the running production Gerrit instance to change instance_type (terraform does a stop/start on the in-place update), but the plan names the required stop/start and the /config/server/version, /review/health, /mcp/ health-recovery gate ONLY on the rollback path -- the forward path defines no downtime window and no post-resize health verification.
findings.location: Operator-Approved Execution Frame -> Terraform plan envelope (`update aws_instance.gerrit`) and Rollback/back-out
scenarios: Operator runs the approved apply; the Gerrit host is stopped for the type change and CI git fetches / MCP / review-bot voting are down for the stop/start window with no pre-declared expectation or post-start health assertion.
The instance comes back but a tenant service (Gerrit JVM, rebar-mcp, review-bot) fails to restart cleanly and no health gate catches it on the forward path.
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the rollback's recovery gate onto the forward apply: after the stop/start, assert Gerrit /config/server/version, /review/health, and /mcp/ respond before re-enabling rebar-autodeploy.timer.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.ec2_cpu_utilization_high wires alarm_actions to aws_sns_topic.alerts and give its threshold + evaluation window (matching the monitoring.tf alarm-window discipline).
evidence: AC4: 'a CPUUtilization alarm exists for sustained host CPU saturation' — states existence only, not alarm_actions/threshold/period
monitoring.tf establishes the notification pattern: aws_sns_topic.alerts + treat_missing_data + evaluation_periods; the new alarm should follow it
ABSENCE: no alarm_actions, comparison threshold, or evaluation window stated for the new alarm in the plan text
findings.finding: AC4's new CPUUtilization alarm is specified only as existing; the plan does not state that it wires to a notification action (the existing aws_sns_topic.alerts SNS topic every other alarm in monitoring.tf uses) nor its trip threshold/evaluation window, so it could be created mute.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria AC4 / Operator-Approved Execution Frame (aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.ec2_cpu_utilization_high)
scenarios: r7g.large saturates CPU under sustained 2x-baseline load post-resize but the new alarm has no SNS action, so no page/email is delivered and the saturation goes unnoticed
findings.suggested_fix: In AC4/the execution frame, state the alarm's CPUUtilization threshold and evaluation_periods/datapoints_to_alarm, and set alarm_actions (and ok_actions) to [aws_sns_topic.alerts.arn] consistent with the other alarms in monitoring.tf.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in the forward Execution Frame that the r7g.large `instance_type` change forces an AWS stop/start (an outage window), and add the same post-resize health-recovery gate (Gerrit /config/server/version, review-bot /review/health, MCP /mcp/) that the rollback path already requires.
evidence: Plan: 'update aws_instance.gerrit (`replace=[]`) — instance type changes from t4g.large to approved r7g.large' and '0 destroy, 0 replace'
Rollback path (only) names the stop/start and health gate: 'allow the required stop/start, then require Gerrit /config/server/version, review-bot /review/health, and MCP /mcp/ response to recover'
AWS behavior: an EC2 instance_type modify requires the instance to be Stopped; the aws provider stops/starts it during the in-place update, so 'replace=[]' does not mean zero downtime
ABSENCE: the forward path has no equivalent post-resize health-recovery assertion
findings.finding: The forward resize is described as an in-place `update aws_instance.gerrit (replace=[])`, but changing an EC2 `instance_type` requires AWS to stop and start the instance; the forward Execution Frame states neither the required stop/start (a Gerrit-serving outage window) nor a forward-path health-recovery verification — the /config/server/version, /review/health, /mcp/ recovery gate appears only in the rollback section.
findings.location: Operator-Approved Execution Frame — forward resize entry (`update aws_instance.gerrit`) and Rollback/back-out paragraph
scenarios: Operator applies the resize expecting no service interruption; Gerrit git-serving/MCP/review-bot go down during the automatic stop/start and no forward health gate confirms recovery
The instance comes back on r7g but a service fails to start and the omission of a forward health check lets the apply be treated as complete
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the forward frame: 'The in-place instance_type update requires AWS to stop and start the instance (brief Gerrit/MCP/review-bot outage); after apply, require Gerrit /config/server/version, review-bot /review/health, and MCP /mcp/ to respond before treating the resize as complete and re-enabling autodeploy.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the attribution method for AC2 (e.g. per-process CPU-time sampling via pidstat/cgroup accounting over a fixed window) and the observable that constitutes 'attributed'.
evidence: AC2: 'The credit burn is attributed across tenants... rather than assumed'
Plan admits: 'no measurement attributes a share of credit burn to it'
CPU credits are an EC2 account-level metric, not per-process
findings.finding: AC2 requires the credit burn be 'attributed across tenants (Gerrit JVM, rebar-mcp, review-bot, opcert, autodeploy, observability)' but specifies no method for attributing CPU-credit burn per process, and the plan itself admits this is currently unmeasured ('no measurement attributes a share of credit burn to it'). The executor cannot act on AC2 without a stated attribution technique.
scenarios: Executor must decide between per-process CPU sampling (pidstat), cgroup accounting, or flame graphs with no guidance.
findings.suggested_fix: State: 'Attribute host CPU via `pidstat -u 60 5` (or per-cgroup CPU accounting) per named tenant, recording each tenant's mean %CPU share on the ticket.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Give AC1 and AC5 concrete proving commands and pass criteria (e.g. AC5: sample rebar-mcp RSS every 10 min for ≥2h post-2685-deploy; 'leak' if monotonic upward slope, 'steady state' if RSS plateaus within ±X%).
evidence: AC5: 'settled by measurement' with no stated measurement or threshold
AC1: 'a fresh reading is taken' with no cited CloudWatch command or acceptance threshold
no proving command in the ACs
findings.finding: AC1 and AC5 lack concrete proving commands/checks. AC1 ('a fresh reading is taken AFTER change 2685 is deployed') and AC5 ('whether rebar-mcp's RSS is a leak or steady state is settled by measurement') describe outcomes but no command that produces the evidence, nor a criterion for what 'settled' means (e.g. RSS trend slope over N hours).
scenarios: Two reviewers disagree on whether rebar-mcp RSS growth over an hour constitutes a 'leak'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile ACs 1-3 with the Operator-Approved Execution Frame: either re-scope AC3 to 'record the rationale for the already-approved r7g.large resize' and make AC1/AC2 confirmatory-only, or state that the resize proceeds regardless of the fresh readings.
evidence: AC3: 'A decision is recorded between the available remedies... move to a non-burstable instance class, resize, reduce tenancy... or accept unlimited surplus charges'
Execution Frame: 'this ticket is approved to execute that resize'
AC4: 'Because the approved remedy is non-burstable r7g.large'
AC1: 'so the decision rests on current data'
findings.finding: The investigation-framed acceptance criteria (AC1 fresh reading 'so the decision rests on current data', AC2 attribute burn 'so the remedy targets the actual consumer', AC3 'a decision is recorded between the available remedies') contradict the Operator-Approved Execution Frame, which states the remedy is already decided, approved, and being executed (r7g.large). An implementer cannot tell whether to gather/attribute data before choosing a remedy or simply execute the pre-approved resize.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria AC1/AC2/AC3 vs Operator-Approved Execution Frame
scenarios: Implementer reads ACs 1-3 as gating the resize on data, but the frame authorizes immediate execution.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite AC3 to 'The rationale and cost basis for the approved r7g.large resize is recorded on the ticket' and reframe AC1/AC2/AC5 as post-hoc confirmations that do not gate execution.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Note in the execution frame that the r7g.large resize removes the burst-credit throttle and surplus charges but is a same-vCPU-count change, so record that if AC2 attributes the burn to a single growing/leaking tenant (e.g. rebar-mcp per AC5), a follow-on tenancy-reduction or right-sizing action may still be required and is not precluded by this resize.
evidence: Summary/AC5: rebar-mcp is 'the largest consumer by a wide margin, which is correlation ... has not been shown to be a leak rather than steady state'; AC5 leaves leak-vs-steady-state 'settled by measurement' -- unresolved.
AC2 asks the burn be 'attributed across tenants ... rather than assumed, so the remedy targets the actual consumer' -- yet AC4 already fixes the remedy as r7g.large.

r7g.large is 2 vCPU (same count as t4g.large); it removes the burst-credit throttle and gives full sustained 2-vCPU entitlement, but does not add cores if the aggregate load is genuinely ~2 vCPU-equivalent driven by a growing tenant.
findings.finding: The remedy (r7g.large, still 2 vCPU) is committed before AC2 (attribute burn across tenants) and AC5 (whether rebar-mcp's 4.45 GB RSS / 47% CPU is a leak or steady state) are resolved; the plan does not reason about whether a same-vCPU-count instance addresses the load if a single tenant is an unbounded consumer.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria AC2/AC4/AC5 vs Operator-Approved Execution Frame
scenarios: Post-resize, rebar-mcp's RSS/CPU keeps climbing (a leak); r7g.large no longer throttles on credits but saturates its 2 vCPU under the same load, and the CPUUtilization alarm added in AC4 fires -- indicating the resize treated the symptom (credit economics) not the driver.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify r7g.large against the measured CPU-bound profile: record why a memory-optimized, same-vCPU-count instance resolves 2x-baseline CPU saturation (e.g. quantify Graviton3 per-core uplift and resulting headroom) and why it was chosen over a compute-optimized alternative such as c7g.large.
evidence: Plan: 'sustained 55-74% across the day against a 30% baseline'; 'Load average 9-12 on 2 vCPU'; 'vmstat showed CPU steal reaching 13%'
Plan: git-upload-pack is CPU-bound ('A full clone needs ~20-28s of CPU')
Retrieved (aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/r7g): R7g are 'designed for memory-intensive workloads'; r7g.large = 2 vCPU / 16 GiB (doit.com/compute r7g.large)
Retrieved (aws.amazon.com compute-optimized): compute-optimized (C-family) instances are 'ideal for compute bound applications'
ABSENCE: plan records no comparison of r7g.large vs a compute-optimized option, and the same 2 vCPU count means CPU relief depends on unstated Graviton3 per-core uplift
findings.finding: The approved remedy (r7g.large) is not justified against the CPU-bound workload the plan itself measures: r7g.large has the same 2 vCPU count as the current t4g.large and belongs to the memory-optimized family, yet the diagnosed deficit is CPU (55-74% util, load 9-12 on 2 vCPU, 13% steal, CPU-bound upload-pack). No prior-art comparison against compute-optimized alternatives (e.g. c7g.large) or a per-core-uplift rationale is recorded.
scenarios: r7g.large deploys, keeps 2 vCPUs, and load 9-12 continues to saturate the two cores — the latency-sensitive surfaces stay degraded and the resize is judged a failure at higher fixed cost
A compute-optimized instance would have relieved CPU saturation more directly and cheaply for a CPU-bound workload
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short remedy-comparison note: current t4g.large is 2 vCPU Graviton2; contrast r7g.large (2 vCPU Graviton3, 16 GiB) vs c7g.large (2 vCPU Graviton3, compute-optimized) for the CPU-bound git-serving workload, stating the per-core uplift assumption and why the extra RAM (7.8->16 GiB, addressing the observed 202 MB-free / no-swap memory pressure) tips the choice to r7g if it does.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Ground AC3's cost-basis decision in AWS's documented 'breakeven CPU usage' analysis, comparing projected monthly unlimited-mode surplus charges against the r7g.large fixed price ($78.18/month) at the observed sustained utilisation.
evidence: Plan AC3: 'A decision is recorded between the available remedies, with its cost basis: move to a non-burstable instance class, resize, reduce tenancy ... or accept unlimited surplus charges as the steady state.'

Retrieved (AWS docs, burstable-performance-instances-unlimited-mode-concepts): 'When determining whether you should use a burstable performance instance in unlimited mode ... or a fixed performance instance ... you need to determine the breakeven CPU usage.'
findings.finding: AC3 requires a decision 'with its cost basis' between burstable-unlimited surplus and fixed-performance classes, but the plan does not reference the established AWS 'breakeven CPU usage' analysis that exists for exactly this burstable-vs-fixed decision.
scenarios: The cost-basis decision is recorded ad hoc without the standard breakeven comparison, so 'accept unlimited surplus' vs 'move to fixed' is not evaluated on comparable terms
